blocks.html: In Grade 2 you learned that 352 is 3 hundreds, 5 tens and 2 ones, and in Grade 3 you saw that 4 × 30 is 12 tens. Now look at one digit as it slides from place to place. Each move to the left makes it worth ten times as much.
A digit in one place is worth 10 times what it would be worth one place to its right. Two places to the left is $10 \times 10 = 100$ times as much.

Ten ones make one ten, ten tens make one hundred, and ten hundreds make one thousand. So each place holds groups that are 10 times bigger than the place before it. A 7 in the tens place means 7 tens, or 70. Move it to the hundreds place and it means 7 hundreds, or 700, which is 10 groups of 70.

blocks.name: placevalue
blocks.cap: Press × 10: every digit slides one place to the left. The 7 goes from 7 tens to 7 hundreds, ten times as much.

blocks.title: The same digit in two places
blocks.q: In $7{,}740$, how many times as much is the first 7 worth as the second 7?
steps: The first 7 is in the thousands place: it is worth $7{,}000$.
The second 7 is in the hundreds place: it is worth $700$.
It is one place to the left, so it is worth 10 times as much: $700 \times 10 = 7{,}000$.

blocks.title: Counting in a bigger unit
steps: One hundred is 10 tens, so 7 hundreds are $7 \times 10 = 70$ tens.

blocks.html: Thinking the 7 in 700 is just "a few more" than the 7 in 70, or that 700 has only 7 tens. The 7 in 700 is worth 10 times the 7 in 70, and 700 holds 70 tens. Check by multiplying: $70 \times 10 = 700$.

blocks.html: You can already read numbers in the thousands, and you know each place is ten times the next. Big numbers up to a million use the same places, grouped in threes.

Commas split a number into periods of three digits: the ones period (hundreds, tens, ones) and the thousands period (hundred thousands, ten thousands, thousands). Read the thousands period, say "thousand", then read the last three digits.

Each period has the same three places: hundreds, tens and ones. The thousands period counts thousands the same way the ones period counts ones. So $305{,}062$ is "three hundred five thousand" and "sixty-two." The comma is where you say "thousand."

blocks.name: placevalue

blocks.title: Words to digits
steps: "Forty thousand": the thousands period is 40, so write $40$, then a comma.
"Six": the ones period must have exactly three digits: hundreds 0, tens 0, ones 6, so $006$.

blocks.title: Expanded form
steps: Read each nonzero digit with its place value: 3 hundred thousands, 5 thousands, 6 tens, 2 ones.
Zeros add nothing, so leave them out of the sum.

blocks.html: Writing "forty thousand six" as $4{,}006$ (a zero dropped) or $400{,}006$ (a zero added). Every period after the first needs exactly three digits, so fill empty places with zeros. Check by reading your number back aloud.

blocks.html: To compare two big numbers, use what you know about reading large numbers and place value. The greatest place matters most.

First count the digits: a whole number with more digits is greater. If they have the same number of digits, compare from the left, place by place. The first place where the digits differ decides which number is greater.

One ten thousand is more than any amount you can make with only thousands, hundreds, tens and ones (the most is $9{,}999$). So a bigger digit in a higher place outweighs everything to its right. That is why you stop at the first difference.

blocks.cap: On a number line, greater numbers sit farther right. B $= 45{,}312$ is to the right of A $= 45{,}231$.

blocks.title: Same number of digits
steps: Both have 5 digits, so start at the left.
Ten thousands: 4 and 4. Thousands: 5 and 5. Still the same.
Hundreds: 3 and 2. Since $3 > 2$, the first number is greater. The tens and ones do not matter now.

blocks.title: Different number of digits
steps: The 5-digit number has a ten thousand, which is more than all of $9{,}876$.

blocks.html: Comparing the last digits, or deciding by the first digit alone when the numbers have different lengths ($9{,}876$ starts with 9 but is less than $10{,}234$). Count digits first, then compare from the left.
The symbol opens toward the greater number: $45{,}312 > 45{,}231$ reads "is greater than"; $9{,}876 < 10{,}234$ reads "is less than."

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you learned rounding to the nearest 10 or 100. The same idea works for any place: find the two "round" numbers on either side, and pick the closer one.

To round to a place, look at the digit just to its right. If it is 5 or more, round up; if it is less than 5, round down. The rounding digit stays or goes up by 1, digits to its left stay the same, and every digit to its right becomes 0.

Rounding to the nearest thousand asks: which thousand is closer? $46{,}372$ sits between $46{,}000$ and $47{,}000$. The halfway point is $46{,}500$. The hundreds digit tells you which side of halfway you are on: 3 hundreds is less than 5 hundreds, so it is closer to $46{,}000$.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: Drag the point. Left of $46{,}500$ it rounds to $46{,}000$; at $46{,}500$ or to the right it rounds to $47{,}000$.

blocks.title: Round down
steps: The thousands digit is 6, so the number is between $46{,}000$ and $47{,}000$.
The digit to its right (hundreds) is 3. That is less than 5, so round down.
Keep 46 thousands; the digits after become zeros.

blocks.title: Round up through a 9
steps: The hundreds digit is 6, which is 5 or more, so round up.
39 thousands plus 1 thousand is 40 thousands: the 9 becomes 0 and the 3 becomes 4.

blocks.html: Rounding one digit at a time from the right: $1{,}448$ to the nearest hundred becomes $1{,}450$ and then $1{,}500$. But $1{,}448$ is closer to $1{,}400$. Only the digit just to the right of the rounding place decides, and digits to the left only change when rounding up carries (as in $39{,}682 \to 40{,}000$). Check: your answer must be the closer of the two round numbers on either side.

blocks.html: You already add and subtract within 1,000 and subtract across zeros. The standard algorithm does the same thing for numbers of any size: one column at a time, starting with the ones.

Line up the digits by place. Add: when a column makes 10 or more, write the ones digit and carry 1 to the next place. Subtract: when the top digit is too small, trade 1 from the next place for 10 in this place.

Carrying and trading never change the amount. Ten ones are one ten, so swapping them only writes the number in standard form. When a place holds 0, you trade from the next place over: 1 thousand becomes 10 hundreds, then 1 of those hundreds becomes 10 tens, and so on.

blocks.title: Subtracting across zeros
steps: Ones: 0 is less than 7, and the tens and hundreds are 0 too. Go to the thousands.
Trade 1 thousand for 10 hundreds, 1 hundred for 10 tens, and 1 ten for 10 ones. The top is now 5 thousands, 9 hundreds, 9 tens, 10 ones.

blocks.html: Taking the smaller digit from the larger one in each column ($6{,}000 - 2{,}347$ becomes $4{,}347$), or trading into a 0 without trading the 0 too. Always add your answer to the number you subtracted: you should get the top number back.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you solved multiplication and division stories about equal groups. Multiplication can also compare two amounts: "Ben has 3 times as many stickers as Ana."
"$k$ times as many as $m$" means $k$ groups the size of $m$, so it is $k \times m$. The equation $15 = 3 \times 5$ can be read "15 is 3 times as many as 5" (and also "15 is 5 times as many as 3").
Draw Ana's 5 stickers as one bar. "3 times as many" means Ben's bar is made of 3 bars that size. Three bars of 5 is $3 \times 5 = 15$. The bigger amount is copies of the smaller one, so you multiply.

steps: The product, 24, is the bigger amount.

blocks.html: Comparison stories come in two kinds. Some say "more than" (an amount added on). Others say "times as many" (copies of an amount), which you met in Times as Many. The words tell you which operation to use.
"$d$ more than" compares by adding or subtracting. "$k$ times as many" compares by multiplying or dividing. To find the smaller amount from the larger one, undo the comparison.

Picture two tapes. With "6 more," the longer tape is the shorter tape plus an extra piece of 6. With "3 times as long," the longer tape is 3 copies of the shorter tape. Different pictures, different math.

steps: "3 times as long" means 3 copies of 6 cm.

blocks.q: A blue ribbon is 18 cm long. A red ribbon is 6 cm longer. How long is the red ribbon?
steps: "6 cm longer" means the blue length plus 6 more.

blocks.q: A dog weighs 45 pounds. That is 5 times as much as a cat. How much does the cat weigh?
steps: 45 is 5 copies of the cat's weight.

blocks.html: Grabbing the numbers and multiplying no matter what the story says. Read the comparison words first: "more" or "less" means add or subtract; "times as" means multiply or divide.

blocks.html: You know that each place is ten times the next. So multiplying by 10 slides every digit one place to the left. Multiplying by 100 is two slides, and by 1,000 is three.

$n \times 10$, $n \times 100$ and $n \times 1{,}000$ move every digit of $n$ one, two or three places left, with zeros filling the empty places. For $6 \times 400$, use the fact $6 \times 4 = 24$: the answer is 24 hundreds, $2{,}400$.

$47 \times 10$ is 10 groups of 47: 10 groups of 4 tens is 40 tens (4 hundreds), and 10 groups of 7 ones is 7 tens. So 4 moves to the hundreds and 7 to the tens: $470$. Each digit lands one place higher. The zero is not "added on"; it holds the empty ones place.

blocks.cap: Press × 10 two or three times and watch 47 become 470, then 4,700, then 47,000.

steps: $1{,}000$ is $10 \times 10 \times 10$, so the digits move 3 places left.

blocks.title: A basic fact with tens and hundreds
steps: Tens times hundreds make thousands, so the product is 20 thousands.

blocks.html: Counting zeros carelessly. In $50 \times 400$, the fact $5 \times 4 = 20$ already ends in 0, so the answer $20{,}000$ has four zeros, not three. Say it in units ("20 thousands") to check.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you split a rectangle to find its area in parts. Now use the same idea for bigger numbers: split a factor by place value, find each part with tens and hundreds facts, and add.
To multiply $4 \times 236$, split $236 = 200 + 30 + 6$. Multiply each part: $4 \times 200$, $4 \times 30$, $4 \times 6$. Then add the partial products.

A rectangle 4 units wide and 236 units long can be cut into three smaller rectangles, 200 long, 30 long and 6 long. Cutting does not change the total area, so the three areas add up to $4 \times 236$. This is the distributive property.

steps: Split: $2{,}000 + 40 + 5$. There are no hundreds, so there is no hundreds part.

blocks.html: The area model finds every partial product. The written method below does the same work in a shorter way: one column at a time, carrying as you go.

Multiply the ones, then the tens, then the hundreds. When a product is 10 or more, write its ones digit and carry the rest to the next place. In the next place, multiply first, then add the carried amount.

In $346 \times 7$, the ones give $6 \times 7 = 42$ ones: 4 tens and 2 ones. The 4 tens join the tens column: $4 \times 7 = 28$ tens, plus the 4 tens makes 32 tens. These are the same partial products as the area model, $2{,}100 + 280 + 42$, added as you go.

blocks.cap: Press Next step to multiply one place at a time. The small blue digits are the carried amounts.

blocks.title: Carrying twice
steps: Tens: $4 \times 7 = 28$, plus 4 carried is 32. Write 2, carry 3.

blocks.html: Forgetting to add the carried amount, so $346 \times 7$ comes out as $2{,}182$. Another slip is adding the carry before multiplying ($4 + 4 = 8$, then $8 \times 7$). Multiply first, then add the carry. Estimate to check: $350 \times 7 = 2{,}450$, close to $2{,}422$.

blocks.html: Now both factors have two digits. The area model still works: split both numbers by place value, and the rectangle has four parts.
For $23 \times 14$, split $23 = 20 + 3$ and $14 = 10 + 4$. Find all four partial products: tens × tens, tens × ones, ones × tens and ones × ones. Then add them.
Each part of 23 must be multiplied by each part of 14, because the whole rectangle is $23$ by $14$. Cutting it both ways makes four rectangles. Leave one out and you lose part of the area.

blocks.html: You know division facts from fact families: $24 \div 4 = 6$ because $6 \times 4 = 24$. But what about $23 \div 4$? Some totals do not split evenly. The part left over is the remainder.

To divide $23 \div 4$, find the biggest multiple of 4 that fits in 23: $5 \times 4 = 20$. The quotient is 5 and the remainder is $23 - 20 = 3$. Write $23 \div 4 = 5$ R 3. The remainder is always less than the divisor.

Make groups of 4 from 23 counters. After 5 groups you have used 20, and 3 are left. If 4 or more were left, you could make another group, so you were not done yet. That is why a remainder must be smaller than the divisor.

blocks.cap: Four groups of 4 are made and 7 counters are left. Is that enough for another group? Press Make a group, then try other group sizes.

blocks.title: Find the quotient and remainder
steps: Count by 4s: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. 24 is too big, so stop at $20 = 5 \times 4$.

blocks.title: Check a remainder
steps: $6 \times 6 + 11 = 47$, so the numbers add up, but 11 is more than 6.
11 left over is enough for another group of 6: one more group, with $11 - 6 = 5$ left.

blocks.html: Stopping too early and leaving a remainder that is as big as the divisor or bigger, like 6 R 11 for $47 \div 6$. Always compare: if the remainder is not less than the divisor, make another group.

blocks.html: You can divide with basic facts and multiply by 10, 100 and 1,000. Put them together to divide numbers like $240 \div 6$ in your head.

Name the number in a bigger unit so a basic fact appears. $240$ is 24 tens, and 24 tens $\div 6 = 4$ tens, so $240 \div 6 = 40$. In the same way, $3{,}600 \div 9$ is 36 hundreds $\div 9$, which is 4 hundreds, or 400.
Sharing 24 ten-dollar bills among 6 people gives each person 4 ten-dollar bills: \$40. The unit (tens) stays the same while you share, just as 24 apples shared by 6 is 4 apples each.

blocks.cap: 240 shown as 24 tens. Shared into 6 equal groups, each group gets 4 tens, which is 40.

blocks.title: A fact that ends in zero

blocks.html: Dropping a zero, as in $3{,}000 \div 5 = 60$. Name the unit out loud ("6 hundreds") and multiply back to check: $60 \times 5 = 300$, not $3{,}000$.

blocks.html: When a dividend is too big for one fact, take it apart. You know how to divide tens and hundreds; partial quotients takes away big, easy groups of the divisor until little is left.

To find $492 \div 4$, subtract easy multiples of 4 (like 100 fours or 10 fours) and keep track of how many groups you took. When what is left is less than 4, add up the groups. That sum is the quotient; what is left is the remainder.

Division asks "how many groups of 4 are in 492?" You can count the groups in chunks: 100 groups use 400, 20 groups use 80, 3 groups use 12. Every 4 is counted once, so $100 + 20 + 3 = 123$ groups in all. The area model shows the same thing: a rectangle with area 492 and one side 4 is built from strips of length 100, 20 and 3.

blocks.name: areamodel
blocks.cap: An area model for $492 \div 4$: the parts $400 + 80 + 12 = 492$, so the missing side is $100 + 20 + 3 = 123$.

blocks.title: With a remainder
steps: Take away 6 fives: $33 - 30 = 3$. Now 3 is less than 5.

blocks.html: Any friendly chunks work. If you take away only 10 fives at a time, you still reach the same answer. Bigger chunks just take fewer steps.

blocks.html: Long division is a tidy way to write partial quotients. Instead of chunks you choose, it divides one place at a time: hundreds, then tens, then ones.

Repeat four moves for each place: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down. Write each quotient digit above the place you just divided. If a place is too small to share, write 0 there and bring down the next digit.

In $618 \div 6$, the 6 hundreds share into 6 groups as 1 hundred each. The 1 ten cannot be shared into 6 groups, so each group gets 0 tens. That 0 holds the tens place, just like the 0 in 103. The 1 ten joins the 8 ones to make 18 ones, and $18 \div 6 = 3$.

blocks.title: A zero in the quotient
steps: Tens: $1 \div 6$ is 0. Write 0. $0 \times 6 = 0$, $1 - 0 = 1$. Bring down 8 to make 18.

blocks.title: Starting with two digits
steps: 1 thousand is too small for 4 groups, so start with 15 hundreds: $15 \div 4 = 3$. $3 \times 4 = 12$, $15 - 12 = 3$. Bring down 7.
Ones: $15 \div 4 = 3$. $3 \times 4 = 12$, $15 - 12 = 3$. Nothing left to bring down.

blocks.html: Skipping the 0: writing $618 \div 6 = 13$. Every place after the first one you divide needs a digit in the quotient. Multiply to check: $13 \times 6 = 78$, nowhere near 618.

blocks.html: A remainder is a real amount: people, inches, dollars. After you divide, read the question again and decide what the remainder means.

There are three common cases. Round up when the leftovers still need something (one more van). Drop it when the leftovers cannot make a whole one (a piece too short to use). Report it when the question asks what is left over.

The quotient counts full groups. In "30 people, 7 per van," $30 \div 7 = 4$ R 2: four vans are full and 2 people are still waiting. They need a van too, so the answer is 5. The math is the same each time; the story decides the answer.

steps: The 2 extra people need a seat, so add a van.

Plan before you calculate: What is the question? What do I need to find first? Write each step as its own equation, using a letter for the unknown if it helps. When you finish, check with an estimate.
A long problem is a chain of short ones. Each step uses the answer to the step before it. Writing the steps keeps the chain in order, and an estimate catches a step that went wrong.

blocks.html: In fact families you saw that $3 \times 4 = 12$ and $12 \div 4 = 3$ go together. Two whole numbers that multiply to make a number are a factor pair of that number.

To list every factor pair of 24, try 1, 2, 3, … in order. Keep each number that divides 24 with no remainder, together with its partner: $1 \times 24$, $2 \times 12$, $3 \times 8$, $4 \times 6$. Stop when the pairs meet in the middle.

Each factor pair is a rectangle of unit squares: 24 squares can make a 1-by-24, 2-by-12, 3-by-8 or 4-by-6 rectangle. Once the short side passes the long side, you are only turning rectangles you already found, so the list is complete.

blocks.cap: Drag the corner to find every rectangle made of exactly 12 squares. Each one is a factor pair of 12.

blocks.title: List all the pairs
blocks.q: Find all the factor pairs of 24.
steps: 5 does not divide 24. The next number, 6, is already in the pair $4 \times 6$, so the pairs have met.

blocks.title: A square number
steps: 5 does not divide 36, and the pairs meet at $6 \times 6$. List 6 only once.

blocks.html: Stopping too soon (missing $4 \times 6$) or forgetting $1 \times 24$. Start at 1 and test every number in order until the pairs meet. Check: the factors should come in partners that multiply back to the number.

blocks.html: Skip-counting gives you multiples. Counting by 6 gives 6, 12, 18, 24, … Each of these is 6 times a whole number. It is the other side of factor pairs.

A multiple of 6 is $6 \times$ a whole number: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, … A factor of 12 divides 12 evenly: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Since $3 \times 4 = 12$, 12 is a multiple of 3 and of 4, and 3 and 4 are factors of 12.

"Factor" and "multiple" describe the same multiplication from two sides. In $3 \times 4 = 12$, the small numbers (3 and 4) are factors, and the product (12) is the multiple. Multiples of a number are never smaller than it; factors are never bigger.

blocks.name: hundredchart
blocks.cap: Multiples of 6 shaded on a hundred chart. Change the skip count to see other patterns.

blocks.title: Factor or multiple?
blocks.q: Which of 2, 3, 24 and 36 are multiples of 12?
steps: 2 and 3 are smaller than 12; they are factors of 12, not multiples.

blocks.html: Mixing the two words, like calling 2 and 3 "multiples of 12." Ask: is it bigger, made by multiplying 12 (a multiple)? Or smaller, dividing into 12 (a factor)?

blocks.html: Some numbers have many factor pairs and some have only one. That difference sorts the counting numbers into primes and composites.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, …). A composite number has more than two factors (4, 6, 8, 9, 10, …). The number 1 has only one factor, so it is neither.

Think of rectangles again. 7 squares make only one rectangle, a 1-by-7 row, so 7 is prime. 9 squares can also make a 3-by-3 square, so 9 is composite. A number is composite as soon as you find any factor pair besides 1 and itself.

steps: You can stop at 7, because $8 \times 8 = 64$ is already more than 53. So the only factors are 1 and 53.

blocks.html: Calling 1 prime, or thinking every odd number is prime. 1 has just one factor, and odd numbers like 9, 15, 21, 51 and 91 are composite. Test small factors (3, 5, 7) before deciding.

blocks.html: Skip-counting and multiples are patterns made by a rule. A rule like "start at 3, add 4" makes a whole list of numbers, and the list often has features the rule never mentions.

To follow a rule, apply it again and again: start at 3 and add 4 to get 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, … To find the 10th number, count the jumps: there are 9 jumps of 4 after the first number, so it is $3 + 9 \times 4 = 39$.

Every number in "start at 3, add 4" is odd. The rule does not say so, but you can explain it: 3 is odd, and adding an even number (4) never changes odd to even. If the rule added an odd number, the list would switch odd, even, odd, even.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you saw with pictures that 1/2 and 2/4 name the same amount. Now you will see why, and get a rule that works for any fraction.

Multiply the numerator and the denominator by the same number, and you get an equivalent fraction: $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{2 \times 4}{3 \times 4} = \dfrac{8}{12}$. The pieces get smaller, there are more of them, and the amount stays the same.

Start with $\dfrac{2}{3}$ of a bar: 2 of 3 equal pieces are shaded. Now cut every piece into 4 smaller pieces. The bar has $3 \times 4 = 12$ pieces, and the shaded part has $2 \times 4 = 8$ of them. Nothing was added or taken away; you only cut. So $\dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{8}{12}$. Multiplying the bottom by 4 makes the pieces 4 times smaller; multiplying the top by 4 counts 4 times as many of them. The two changes cancel out.

blocks.html: You can make equivalent fractions by multiplying. Going the other way, dividing the top and bottom by a common factor, uses fewer, larger pieces.

A fraction is in simplest form when the only number that divides both the numerator and the denominator is 1. To simplify $\dfrac{8}{12}$, divide both by a common factor: $\dfrac{8 \div 4}{12 \div 4} = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Dividing undoes the cutting. In $\dfrac{8}{12}$, put every 4 small pieces back together into one bigger piece. 12 pieces become 3, and the 8 shaded pieces become 2. Same amount, bigger pieces: $\dfrac{2}{3}$.

blocks.html: You can already compare fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator. For other pairs, a quick trick is to compare each one with a benchmark: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ or 1.

A fraction is more than $\dfrac{1}{2}$ when its numerator is more than half its denominator, so when double the numerator is more than the denominator. It is more than 1 when the numerator is more than the denominator. If one fraction is below a benchmark and the other is above, you know which is bigger.

Half of 8 eighths is 4 eighths. $\dfrac{5}{8}$ has 5 eighths, more than half, while $\dfrac{2}{5}$ has 2 fifths, less than half of 5 fifths. Since one is above the middle and one is below, $\dfrac{5}{8} > \dfrac{2}{5}$, and you never needed a common denominator.

To compare $\dfrac{2}{3}$ and $\dfrac{3}{5}$, rename both with a common denominator, such as 15: $\dfrac{10}{15}$ and $\dfrac{9}{15}$. Now the pieces are the same size, so the one with more pieces is greater: $\dfrac{2}{3} > \dfrac{3}{5}$. Both fractions must refer to the same whole.
Comparing thirds with fifths is like comparing 2 large slices with 3 small slices. Cutting both into fifteenths makes all the slices the same size; then you only count.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you built fractions from unit fractions: $\dfrac{3}{4}$ is three pieces of size $\dfrac{1}{4}$. Turn that around and you can break a fraction into parts in many ways.

A fraction can be split into a sum of fractions with the same denominator, as long as the numerators add up: $\dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{3}{8} = \dfrac{2}{8} + \dfrac{3}{8}$. Mixed numbers split the same way: $2\dfrac{1}{8} = 1 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{8}{8} + \dfrac{8}{8} + \dfrac{1}{8}$.
$\dfrac{5}{8}$ is just 5 eighth-pieces. You can sort 5 pieces into piles any way you like (1 and 4, or 2 and 3, or 1, 1 and 3) and you still have 5 eighths.

blocks.html: If you can break a fraction into parts, you can put parts together. Adding fractions with the same denominator is counting pieces of the same size.

To add or subtract fractions with the same denominator, add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator: $\dfrac{1}{5} + \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{3}{5}$ and $\dfrac{7}{8} - \dfrac{3}{8} = \dfrac{4}{8}$.

The denominator names the size of the pieces (fifths); the numerator counts them. 1 fifth and 2 fifths make 3 fifths, the same way 1 apple and 2 apples make 3 apples. Putting pieces together does not change their size, so the denominator stays 5.

$2\dfrac{1}{3}$ (a mixed number) and $\dfrac{7}{3}$ (a fraction greater than 1) name the same amount. Mixed to fraction: wholes × denominator, plus the numerator: $2 \times 3 + 1 = 7$, so $\dfrac{7}{3}$. Fraction to mixed: divide, $7 \div 3 = 2$ R 1, so $2\dfrac{1}{3}$.

Each whole is 3 thirds. Two wholes are $3 + 3 = 6$ thirds, and the extra $\dfrac{1}{3}$ makes 7 thirds. Going back, every 3 thirds you can group make one whole; 7 thirds make 2 groups with 1 third left over.

blocks.html: Mixed numbers have a whole part and a fraction part. To add or subtract them, use like fractions for the fraction parts and whole-number math for the wholes. Sometimes you need to trade, just as you turned wholes into fractions.

Add or subtract wholes with wholes and fractions with fractions. When adding, if the fractions make 1 or more, regroup a whole. When subtracting, if the first fraction is too small, trade 1 whole for $\dfrac{d}{d}$ (like $\dfrac{5}{5}$) first.

$3\dfrac{1}{5}$ is 3 wholes and 1 fifth. To take away $\dfrac{3}{5}$ you need more fifths, so cut one whole into 5 fifths: now you have 2 wholes and 6 fifths, still the same amount. It is the same idea as trading 1 ten for 10 ones, except a whole is 5 fifths, not 10.

steps: $\dfrac{1}{5}$ is less than $\dfrac{3}{5}$, so trade 1 whole for $\dfrac{5}{5}$: $3\dfrac{1}{5} = 2\dfrac{6}{5}$.

Decide what the story does. Putting amounts together (in all, total, altogether) means add. Taking away, finding what is left, or comparing (how much more, how much farther) means subtract. Then keep the denominator and work with the numerators.

A fraction story is a whole-number story with fraction-sized pieces. "It rained 3 eighths of an inch, then 4 eighths more" is the same as "3 drops, then 4 more drops," only the drops are eighths. A tape diagram shows the parts and the whole.

blocks.html: In Grade 3, multiplication meant equal groups: $3 \times 4$ is 3 groups of 4. The same meaning works when each group is a fraction, and you already know how to add like fractions.

$3 \times \dfrac{2}{5}$ means 3 groups of $\dfrac{2}{5}$: $\dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{2}{5} + \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5}$. Multiply the whole number by the numerator and keep the denominator: $3 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = \dfrac{3 \times 2}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5}$.

$\dfrac{2}{5}$ is 2 pieces of size $\dfrac{1}{5}$. Three groups of 2 pieces is 6 pieces, and each piece is still a fifth. So $3 \times \dfrac{2}{5} = 6 \times \dfrac{1}{5} = \dfrac{6}{5}$. Nothing makes the pieces smaller, so the denominator does not change.

blocks.html: Tenths and hundredths are the fractions that money and measuring use most. You know how to make equivalent fractions by multiplying; here the multiplier is always 10.

One tenth is 10 hundredths, so $\dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{30}{100}$. To add tenths and hundredths, first write the tenths as hundredths: $\dfrac{3}{10} + \dfrac{4}{100} = \dfrac{30}{100} + \dfrac{4}{100} = \dfrac{34}{100}$.

Cut a square into 10 strips: each strip is one tenth. Cut every strip into 10 small squares and the whole has 100 squares, so each strip is 10 hundredths. Three strips are 30 small squares: $\dfrac{3}{10} = \dfrac{3 \times 10}{10 \times 10} = \dfrac{30}{100}$.

blocks.html: Decimals are another way to write tenths and hundredths. They extend the place-value chart you know from each place is ten times the next to the right of the ones.

The first place after the decimal point is tenths; the second is hundredths. So $0.3 = \dfrac{3}{10}$, $0.03 = \dfrac{3}{100}$, and $0.47 = \dfrac{47}{100}$ (4 tenths and 7 hundredths). A whole number goes before the point: $2\dfrac{35}{100} = 2.35$.

The places keep the same pattern: moving right, each place is one tenth of the place before it. One one splits into 10 tenths, and one tenth splits into 10 hundredths. The decimal point marks where the ones end, so each digit after it knows its size by its position.

blocks.html: To compare decimals, use the place value from writing decimals. It works just like comparing whole numbers: start at the greatest place.

Compare the whole numbers first, then the tenths, then the hundredths. It helps to write both decimals with two places: $0.3 = 0.30$. Now $0.30$ and $0.25$ are 30 hundredths and 25 hundredths, so $0.3 > 0.25$.

A 0 at the end of a decimal adds 0 hundredths, so it does not change the amount: 3 tenths is exactly 30 hundredths. Writing both with hundredths makes the pieces the same size, and then you can compare like whole numbers. Both decimals must refer to the same whole.

blocks.html: A foot is 12 inches, an hour is 60 minutes, and a kilogram is 1,000 grams. Changing a big unit into a small one is multiplication, the same kind you did in multiplying by 10, 100 and 1,000.

To change a larger unit into a smaller unit, multiply by how many small units are in one large unit: $3$ feet $= 3 \times 12 = 36$ inches; $2$ kg $= 2 \times 1{,}000 = 2{,}000$ g. The number gets bigger because the unit got smaller.

Each foot becomes 12 inches, so 3 feet become 3 groups of 12 inches. Smaller units fit more times into the same length, so you need more of them. A table makes the pattern easy to see: each row adds one more group.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you found area and perimeter by counting squares and adding sides. With two-digit multiplication you can use formulas for rectangles of any size.

For a rectangle with length $l$ and width $w$: area $A = l \times w$ (square units) and perimeter $P = 2 \times l + 2 \times w$ (units). To find a missing side, work backward: $w = A \div l$, or take $2 \times l$ away from the perimeter and halve what is left.

Area counts unit squares: $w$ rows of $l$ squares is $l \times w$. Perimeter walks around the outside: along a length, a width, the other length and the other width. Opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, so that is two lengths and two widths.

blocks.html: In Grade 2 you described shapes by their sides and corners. Geometry gives the parts of shapes exact names, starting with points and straight paths.

A point is an exact spot, named by a letter. A segment $\overline{AB}$ is the straight path between two endpoints. A ray $\overrightarrow{CD}$ starts at an endpoint C and goes on forever through D. A line $\overleftrightarrow{EF}$ goes on forever in both directions.

The arrowheads in a drawing mean "keeps going." A segment has no arrows because it stops at both ends. A ray has one arrow, so its name must say where it starts: $\overrightarrow{CD}$ starts at C, while $\overrightarrow{DC}$ would start at D and point the other way. A line has no start, so $\overleftrightarrow{EF}$ and $\overleftrightarrow{FE}$ name the same line.

blocks.html: Two rays that share an endpoint make an angle. The shared endpoint is the vertex. What does the size of an angle measure? Not the length of its sides: the amount of turn between them.

Imagine one ray turning around the vertex until it lands on the other ray. A full turn is $360^\circ$, so one degree is $\dfrac{1}{360}$ of a full turn. A quarter turn is $90^\circ$, a half turn is $180^\circ$, and an angle that turns through 50 one-degree angles measures $50^\circ$.

To measure, you need a unit, just like inches for length. The unit for turning is the one-degree angle: split a full circle into 360 equal slices, and each slice is 1 degree. Measuring an angle means counting how many of those slices fit inside it. Making the rays longer does not add any slices.

blocks.html: Thinking longer sides make a bigger angle. The size of an angle is how far it opens, not how long its rays are drawn. You could extend both rays forever and the turn would stay the same.

blocks.html: Now that you know what an angle measures, you can sort angles by comparing them with a right angle, the square corner of a sheet of paper.

An acute angle is less than $90^\circ$. A right angle is exactly $90^\circ$ (a square corner, often marked with a small square). An obtuse angle is between $90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. A straight angle is exactly $180^\circ$: its rays form a line.

A right angle is a quarter turn. Anything that turns less than a quarter turn fits inside a square corner (acute); anything more sticks out past it (obtuse). A half turn, $180^\circ$, points the rays in opposite directions, which makes a straight line.

blocks.q: At 3:00, what kind of angle do the clock hands make?
steps: From 12 to 3 is a quarter turn: $90^\circ$.

blocks.html: Judging by how the angle is turned on the page. A right angle tipped on its side is still $90^\circ$, and an acute angle with long rays is still acute. Hold a square corner against it to check.

blocks.html: You can sort angles as acute, right or obtuse. A protractor measures them exactly, in degrees. It has two scales, and choosing the right one is the whole trick.

Put the protractor's center point on the vertex. Line up the 0 line with one ray. Find the scale that reads 0 on that ray, and follow it to the other ray. Then check: an acute angle must be less than $90^\circ$, an obtuse angle more.

Each scale counts degrees from one side. The outer scale starts at 0 on the right; the inner scale starts at 0 on the left. Both are correct, but only one of them starts where your angle starts. The two readings always add to $180^\circ$, so the wrong one is the other part of a straight line.

blocks.title: Outer scale
blocks.q: An angle's first ray lies along the 0 on the right. The second ray crosses the outer scale at 70. What is the angle?
steps: The angle starts at 0 on the outer scale, so read the outer scale.
It is less than a right angle, so 70 (not 110) makes sense.

blocks.title: Inner scale
blocks.q: An angle opens from the left. Its second ray crosses the scales at 40 (inner) and 140 (outer). What is the angle?
steps: The angle starts at 0 on the left, which is the inner scale.
The angle looks acute, so $40^\circ$ makes sense.

blocks.html: Reading the wrong scale, so an acute angle is reported as $130^\circ$. Always decide first whether the angle is acute or obtuse, then pick the reading that agrees.

blocks.html: You can measure an angle with a protractor. When a ray splits an angle into two parts, the measures behave like lengths: the parts add up to the whole.

If ray BC is inside $\angle ABD$, then $\angle ABC + \angle CBD = \angle ABD$. To find a missing part, subtract the known part from the whole. Remember the wholes you know: a right angle is $90^\circ$ and a straight angle is $180^\circ$.

Angle measures count one-degree turns. Turning $35^\circ$ and then $50^\circ$ more in the same direction is $85^\circ$ of turning in all, as long as the two angles sit side by side with no gap and no overlap.

blocks.html: You know lines and right angles. Two lines in the same flat plane either never meet or cross at exactly one point, and the way they cross gives them names.

Parallel lines never meet, no matter how far they go; they stay the same distance apart ($\overleftrightarrow{AB} \parallel \overleftrightarrow{CD}$). Perpendicular lines cross at a right angle ($\overleftrightarrow{AB} \perp \overleftrightarrow{CD}$). Many crossing lines are neither.

Parallel lines point in exactly the same direction. On a dot grid, that means they take the same steps: if one goes 2 over and 1 up, so does the other, so the gap between them never shrinks. Perpendicular lines make four square corners where they cross. On the grid, "2 over, 1 up" is perpendicular to "1 back, 2 up": a quarter turn of the same steps.

steps: Top and bottom are parallel; left and right are parallel: 2 pairs.
Each corner is a right angle, so sides that meet at a corner are perpendicular.
blocks.a: 2 pairs of parallel sides; 4 corners where sides are perpendicular

blocks.html: Thinking two lines are parallel just because they have not met yet on the page. Lines go on forever; if their directions differ even a little, they cross somewhere. Check their steps on the grid.

blocks.html: In Grade 3 you met kinds of quadrilaterals. Now you can sort shapes using two new tools: parallel and perpendicular sides and the kinds of angles they have.

Triangles are sorted by their largest angle: acute (all angles acute), right (one right angle) or obtuse (one obtuse angle). Quadrilaterals are sorted by parallel sides and right angles: a trapezoid has a pair of parallel sides, a parallelogram two pairs, a rectangle two pairs and 4 right angles, a rhombus 4 equal sides, and a square is both a rectangle and a rhombus.

A name is a promise about attributes. "Rectangle" promises 4 right angles. A square keeps that promise (and also has equal sides), so every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square. The best name is the one that promises the most.

blocks.html: After sorting shapes, here is one more attribute to look for: does the shape have a mirror line?
A line of symmetry folds a shape so the two halves match exactly. A rectangle has 2 (across its middles), a square has 4, an equilateral triangle has 3, and some shapes have none.

Folding along a line flips each point to the same distance on the other side. A line is a line of symmetry only if every corner lands exactly on another corner. For a rectangle's diagonal, the corners land outside the rectangle, so the diagonal is not a line of symmetry.

steps: Fold across the middle up-and-down and side-to-side: 2 lines.
Fold along each diagonal: the corners match, 2 more lines.

blocks.q: Is the line from the top corner of an isosceles triangle to the middle of its base a line of symmetry?
steps: The two equal sides fold onto each other.
The base's halves match, and the top corner stays on the line.
